system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2178-07-03 14:45:00 to 2178-07-06 16:56:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with a symptomatic urinary tract infection caused by multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae, complicated by acute delirium and myoclonic jerks. He was started on cefepime, which was later changed to imipenem based on culture results. His mental status improved rapidly with appropriate antibiotic therapy. A groin rash was diagnosed as candidiasis and treated with topical ketoconazole. His foley catheter was exchanged to reduce infection risk. He completed a course of IV antibiotics and was discharged to extended care for 10 days of daily ertapenem injections. His chronic conditions, including diastolic heart failure, benign prostatic hypertrophy, and a right renal mass, remained stable. Blood cultures remained negative, and imaging showed no new acute findings.
problems: Infection and inflammatory reaction due to indwelling urinary catheter
Malignant neoplasm of kidney, except pelvis
Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Hypertrophy (benign) of prostate without urinary obstruction and other lower urinary tract symptom (LUTS)
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Friedländer's bacillus infection in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site

PROCEDURE DETAILS:
The patient was brought to the angiographic suite and placed 
supine on the
table. A preprocedure timeout was performed using three patient 
identifiers. The skin of the right upper extremity was prepped 
and draped in the usual sterile fashion including the indwelling 
single-lumen PICC catheter.
An initial scout image demonstrated the PICC to be in the mid 
axillary line. A nitinol wire was advanced through the PICC; 
however, this would not pass more centrally in the mid axillary 
line. The PICC was withdrawn and a 4.5 ___ peel-away sheath 
was advanced over the wire. A 5 ___ Kumpe catheter was 
advanced over the wire and we attempted to inject contrast; 
however, contrast could not be injected via the catheter. The 
catheter was gradually withdrawn until there was opacification 
of an axillary vein; however, clearly a false tract had been 
created. So, this catheter was removed and firm manual 
compression was applied for 5 minutes. Following this, we 
attempted to place a new PICC. A second right upper extremity 
vein was selected; this appeared to be the right basilic vein. 1 
cc of lidocaine was infiltrated into the skin and subcutaneous 
tissues for local anesthesia. Using direct ultrasound 
visualization, a micropuncture needle was advanced into the 
vein. Ultrasound images were saved prior to and after 
venopuncture, confirming patency of the vein. A nitinol wire 
advanced through the micropuncture needle without difficulty. A 
small skin incision was made and the micropuncture needle was 
exchanged for a 4.5 ___ peel-away sheath. The nitinol wire 
was advanced readily into the IVC confirming venous positioning. 
The wire was withdrawn into the SVC to estimate the length of 
required tubing. A new single-lumen Power PICC was selected, 
flushed and cut to 42 cm. This advanced over the
nitinol wire without difficulty. The peel-away sheath was 
gradually removed
as the catheter was advanced. The nitinol wire was removed. 
Following completion of this maneuver, the tip of the catheter 
was in the distal SVC.
The catheter was secured to the skin with a StatLock device. The 
catheter was aspirating and flushing without difficulty. There 
were no immediate
post-procedure complications. IMPRESSION: Unsuccessful 
repositioning of a PICC, a new single-lumen Power PICC has been 
placed with the tip in the distal SVC. The catheter has been 
flushed and is ready for use.

PROCEDURE DETAILS:
The patient was brought to the angiographic suite and placed 
supine on the
table. A preprocedure timeout was performed using three patient 
identifiers. The skin of the right upper extremity was prepped 
and draped in the usual sterile fashion including the indwelling 
single-lumen PICC catheter.
An initial scout image demonstrated the PICC to be in the mid 
axillary line. A nitinol wire was advanced through the PICC; 
however, this would not pass more centrally in the mid axillary 
line. The PICC was withdrawn and a 4.5 ___ peel-away sheath 
was advanced over the wire. A 5 ___ Kumpe catheter was 
advanced over the wire and we attempted to inject contrast; 
however, contrast could not be injected via the catheter. The 
catheter was gradually withdrawn until there was opacification 
of an axillary vein; however, clearly a false tract had been 
created. So, this catheter was removed and firm manual 
compression was applied for 5 minutes. Following this, we 
attempted to place a new PICC. A second right upper extremity 
vein was selected; this appeared to be the right basilic vein. 1 
cc of lidocaine was infiltrated into the skin and subcutaneous 
tissues for local anesthesia. Using direct ultrasound 
visualization, a micropuncture needle was advanced into the 
vein. Ultrasound images were saved prior to and after 
venopuncture, confirming patency of the vein. A nitinol wire 
advanced through the micropuncture needle without difficulty. A 
small skin incision was made and the micropuncture needle was 
exchanged for a 4.5 ___ peel-away sheath. The nitinol wire 
was advanced readily into the IVC confirming venous positioning. 
The wire was withdrawn into the SVC to estimate the length of 
required tubing. A new single-lumen Power PICC was selected, 
flushed and cut to 42 cm. This advanced over the
nitinol wire without difficulty. The peel-away sheath was 
gradually removed
as the catheter was advanced. The nitinol wire was removed.

was in the distal SVC.
The catheter was secured to the skin with a StatLock device. The 
catheter was aspirating and flushing without difficulty. There 
were no immediate
post-procedure complications. IMPRESSION: Unsuccessful 
repositioning of a PICC, a new single-lumen Power PICC has been 
placed with the tip in the distal SVC. The catheter has been 
flushed and is ready for use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. You're in the hospital because you've been feeling confused and have pain when urinating. Can you tell me how you're feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not sure… I’ve been tired and my head feels foggy. And yes, it burns when I pee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your daughter mentioned you’ve been more disoriented over the last few days. That, along with the burning, suggests a urinary tract infection, especially since you have a catheter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had these infections before. They always make me confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s common, especially with your history. We’ve started you on an antibiotic called Zosyn through your IV. It covers the types of bacteria you’ve had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe? I remember last time they changed my meds because of resistance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. You had a resistant Klebsiella before. We gave imipenem in the ER, but we’re switching to Zosyn because it’s effective and safer long-term based on your past cultures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also replaced your catheter today. That helps reduce infection risk and gives us a cleaner sample.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It felt a bit uncomfortable, but I understand why.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you lidocaine jelly to help. We’ll keep using that if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound on your left leg because it looked swollen. Good news—it showed no blood clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t even notice the swelling. Is that from the heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. You have heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, so fluid can build up. But the swelling improved, so we’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My furosemide helps with that, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re on 20 mg daily, which we’ll continue. Your labs today are stable—no signs of dehydration or kidney issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Clearer in my head. Still tired, but not as foggy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your mental status is improving, which tells us the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will I be able to go back to rehab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to finish a full 10-day course of IV antibiotics. We’re going to place a PICC line so you can get them at rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s a PICC line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a long IV line placed in your arm that goes to a large vein near your heart. It’s safe and lets you get antibiotics without daily needle sticks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get numbing medicine, so it shouldn’t be painful. A radiology team will do it with ultrasound guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your urine culture came back. The bacteria are sensitive to Zosyn, so we’re staying on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No surprises this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s good news. The bacteria are responding well. Your white blood cell count is normal too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my confusion is gone. I know where I am now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That was delirium from the infection. It’s resolving, which is a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my sore spot on the penis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping an eye on that 2 cm area of redness. It’s likely from the catheter. We’ll keep it clean and use the lidocaine jelly for comfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my back sore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The wound care team checked your sacral ulcer. It’s a stage II pressure sore. They’re using Mepilex dressing, which helps it heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They said I need to keep moving as much as I can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. That helps prevent new sores. You’re doing well with transfers—we want you to keep building strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day we discharge you to rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Did the PICC line go in okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was placed yesterday. The first attempt didn’t work, but they successfully placed a new one in your right arm. It’s in the right spot and working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No complications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: None. They used ultrasound and confirmed placement. You’ll get Zosyn every 8 hours for 7 more days at rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All continued as before. We switched your metoprolol to the once-daily succinate form for better heart protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. What about my kidney mass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s still there, but stable on recent scans. You have a follow-up with urology. No treatment needed now unless it changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my DNR status?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s documented. You’ll remain DNR/DNI, and that will go with you to rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Just remember: finish all antibiotics, keep up with wound care, and work on standing and transferring. You’ll be back home soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your labs this morning look good. Kidney function, blood count, everything is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send a full summary to your rehab team. They’ll continue your care exactly as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And that’s the goal. Infection’s under control, your mind is clear, and you’re ready to keep recovering where you were.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team will take you in about 30 minutes. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think you’ve covered everything. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you only if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in before you leave. How’s your pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Minimal. I used acetaminophen once yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Keep it on hand. And keep using the ketoconazole on your groin as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t forgotten.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’ve done really well this admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks to you and the team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels back to rehab. We’ll be in touch with your doctors there.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with altered mental status and dysuria, found to have a complicated urinary tract infection likely due to his chronic indwelling catheter. He was treated with intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam after an initial dose of imipenem, with improvement in mental status and resolution of delirium. His catheter was replaced to reduce infection risk, and a new PICC line was placed for continued antibiotic therapy. Left lower extremity swelling resolved without evidence of DVT. Chronic conditions including diastolic heart failure, benign prostatic hypertrophy, type 2 diabetes, and a right renal mass remained stable. He was discharged to extended care to complete a 10-day course of IV antibiotics and continue wound care for a stage II sacral pressure ulcer and penile shaft inflammation.
